blocks.text: This module opener covers manual evaluation, a human reviewer directly judging the actual quality of model responses, the foundational form of evaluation every automated technique covered later in this module ultimately gets calibrated against.

This topic covers why manual review remains essential even as automated techniques become available, designing a clear rubric for consistent judgments, sampling a representative subset rather than reviewing everything, and the real cost and scaling limits manual review runs into.
1. What Manual Evaluation Means

blocks.alt: Building on the completed Prompt Security module, Prompt Evaluation opens with manual evaluation

blocks.text: Manual evaluation means a human reviewer directly reading and judging model responses against defined criteria, rather than relying on an automated metric or another model to make that judgment.

blocks.alt: A human reviewer judges actual response quality directly

blocks.text: 2. Why Manual Review Remains Essential

Even as automated evaluation techniques, covered in the next topic, become increasingly capable, manual review remains the ultimate ground truth for genuinely subjective or nuanced quality judgments, tone appropriateness, subtle factual correctness, whether a response actually feels helpful to a real person, that automated metrics can only approximate.
3. Designing a Manual Review Rubric

blocks.alt: No defined rubric produces inconsistent judgments, a clear, defined rubric produces consistent judgments

blocks.text: This connects directly to the specificity principle covered throughout this course, asking a reviewer to simply judge if this good leaves too much room for inconsistent, subjective interpretation, a clear rubric, specific criteria and a defined scale for each, produces judgments that are consistent both across different reviewers and across time.
4. Sampling a Representative Subset

blocks.alt: Reviewing every single response is compared against reviewing a representative sample

blocks.text: This connects directly to the A/B testing sample size considerations covered in an earlier module, manually reviewing every single response a system produces rarely scales, reviewing a representative, randomly selected sample gives a reliable signal about overall quality without the impossible cost of exhaustive review.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Approach","Tradeoff"],"rows":[["Review every response","Most thorough, rarely scales in practice"],["Review a representative sample","Scalable, still gives a reliable quality signal"]]}

blocks.text: 5. Inter-Rater Agreement Between Reviewers

blocks.alt: Reviewer A and reviewer B both judge, and agreement between them gets checked

blocks.text: When more than one person reviews the same responses, checking how much their judgments actually agree, called inter-rater agreement, reveals whether the rubric is genuinely clear and consistently interpretable, low agreement between reviewers usually signals the rubric itself needs to be more specific, not that the reviewers are doing a poor job.

blocks.title: Low agreement is a rubric problem more often than a reviewer problem
blocks.content: When two thoughtful reviewers following the same rubric reach meaningfully different judgments, the more common root cause is ambiguity in the rubric itself rather than a genuine difference in reviewer skill or attention.

blocks.text: 6. The Cost and Scaling Limits

blocks.alt: Manual review cost scales linearly with volume

blocks.text: Manual evaluation cost scales roughly linearly with how many responses need review, doubling the volume roughly doubles the review effort required, this real, direct cost is exactly why automated evaluation, covered in the next topic, and sampling both matter so much for evaluating at any real scale.
7. Manual Evaluation as the Foundation for Automation

blocks.alt: Manual evaluation forms the foundation that automated evaluation builds on next

blocks.text: This sets up the next topic directly, automated evaluation techniques are generally validated by checking how well they agree with careful manual review on a representative sample, manual evaluation is not replaced by automation, it becomes the calibration standard automation is measured against.
8. A Worked Manual Evaluation Example

A team evaluating a customer support assistant has two trained reviewers independently score a sample of one hundred responses against a five point rubric covering accuracy, tone, and completeness, checking agreement between the two reviewers before trusting the aggregated scores as a reliable signal of actual system quality.
9. When Manual Evaluation Alone Is Not Enough

For a system running at genuinely high volume, or one needing rapid feedback during iterative development, covered in the earlier Prompt Iteration topic, manual evaluation alone is too slow and expensive to run on every single change, this is exactly the gap automated evaluation, covered next, exists to fill.
Worked Example

A team initially asks a single reviewer to informally judge whether responses seem good, producing inconsistent, hard to compare results from one review session to the next, since good was never actually defined.

Introducing a specific rubric with defined criteria and scales, and having two reviewers independently score the same sample to check agreement, produces evaluation results the team can actually trust and compare consistently across different versions of their system over time.
Common Mistakes

items: Asking a reviewer to judge overall quality without a specific, defined rubric to judge against
Attempting to manually review every single response instead of a representative sample
Not checking inter-rater agreement when more than one reviewer is involved
Relying purely on manual evaluation for a system that genuinely needs fast, frequent feedback during iteration

blocks.text: Practice

Design a simple three criteria rubric for a task you are familiar with, apply it yourself to five example responses, then have someone else apply the same rubric to the same five responses, and compare how closely your judgments actually agree.
Key Takeaway

Manual evaluation, a human reviewer judging response quality against a clear, defined rubric, remains the foundational ground truth for evaluating genuinely subjective or nuanced quality, best applied to a representative sample rather than every response, and it serves as the calibration standard the automated evaluation techniques covered next are ultimately measured against.
